content:
I’m sorry—that’s a gut-punch. The inheritance-tax idea had a very strong moral logic: large inheritances are unearned wealth, they are concentrated, and climate costs should not be carried mainly by ordinary households through energy bills, transport prices, or delayed public investment. If I had to salvage as much of the JUSO initiative as possible, I would not try to repackage the same vote as a blunt “inheritance tax.” I would build a narrower, more Swiss, more defensible instrument: a **large-estate climate contribution**.

## The compromise I would design: an “Erbklima-Beitrag”

The name matters. I would avoid “Erbsteuer” and use something like:

> **Klimaschutz-Beitrag bei grossen Erbschaften**  
> or  
> **Erbklima-Beitrag**

The core idea: **large inheritances pay a one-time contribution toward climate protection, but the design removes the main reasons Swiss voters reject taxes.**

### 1. High threshold: do not touch ordinary family estates

I would set the threshold high enough that the message is unmistakable:

> “Your parents’ house, a small family business, savings from a lifetime of work? Not the target. Very large inherited fortunes: yes.”

For example:

| Net estate after debts | Contribution |
|---|---:|
| Up to CHF 5 million | 0% |
| CHF 5–20 million | 5% |
| Above CHF 20 million | 10% |

That is still a substantial climate finance lever, but it is much harder to sell as “the tax on Swiss families.” It becomes “a climate legacy contribution from the very top.”

If you wanted to keep even more of the original ambition, you could use a slightly lower threshold, but politically the safest version is one where **95%+ of inheritances are unaffected**.

### 2. No double taxation: solve the cantonal objection

Switzerland already has cantonal and municipal inheritance taxes in many cases. A federal inheritance tax without proper coordination sounds like Bern stacking another tax on top of the cantons. That is a major vulnerability.

The compromise should say:

- The federal climate contribution is **credited against cantonal/municipal inheritance tax** on the same assets, or
- It **replaces** the overlapping cantonal inheritance tax, with cantons receiving a share of the revenue or compensation to protect their fiscal position.

The voter message should be simple:

> “No double tax. The federal contribution does not sit on top of cantonal inheritance tax. Cantons are compensated.”

That does not just make the policy more fair; it makes it politically survivable.

### 3. Protect family farms and family businesses, but not as a loophole

The strongest counterargument to inheritance taxes in Switzerland will be: “This will kill family farms and small family businesses.” That objection is understandable, even if it is also often exaggerated.

A serious compromise should include real protections:

- **Family farms and family businesses** receive a major exemption or deferral if the business continues to operate for a set period, say five years.
- If the business is sold within that period, the deferred contribution becomes due.
- The protection should apply to **productive assets**, not to a financial fortune temporarily parked in a shell company.

The message:

> “We are not taxing productive family assets that create jobs. We are asking large unearned wealth to pay for the climate its heirs will inherit.”

### 4. Make the climate purpose concrete and time-limited

Swiss voters are often skeptical of earmarking, especially if it sounds rigid. But if the money is for climate, it should be transparent, visible, and limited.

I would tie the revenue to a **Federal Climate and Adaptation Fund** with a clear allocation formula, for example:

- **50% decarbonization**: public transport, grid expansion, building retrofits, heat pumps, industrial transition, public procurement.
- **30% adaptation and resilience**: flood protection, heat protection, water management, nature-based solutions, infrastructure resilience.
- **20% social compensation**: support for households and businesses hit hardest by climate policy, energy poverty, just transition.

And crucially:

> The contribution lasts for **10 years**, then voters decide again based on results.

That makes it less permanent, less fearful, and more accountable.

### 5. Pair it with a broader climate package

The inheritance contribution should not be presented as “the only way” to pay for climate action. That makes it an easy target: “This won’t cut emissions,” “This is too little,” “This is just a tax.”

Instead, it should be part of a package:

- CO2 tax, with revenue returned or used for public transport and energy transition;
- corporate climate fees or border carbon adjustment where necessary;
- building retrofit programs;
- public transport investment;
- ending unnecessary fossil subsidies;
- public procurement standards;
- climate adaptation funding.

The inheritance contribution is not the whole engine. It is the **fairness instrument**: the part that says the wealthiest should carry a visible share.

## The one-page version

If I were drafting the popular initiative text, I would make it look like this:

> **Large inheritances pay a climate contribution**  
>  
> Inheritances above CHF 5 million pay a one-time contribution of 5% to 10%.  
>   
> The contribution is credited against cantonal and municipal inheritance taxes. There is no double taxation. Cantons receive a fair share or compensation.  
>   
> Family farms and family businesses are protected if they continue to operate.  
>   
> The money goes to a federal climate fund for 10 years: decarbonization, adaptation, and support for those who bear the costs.  
>   
> The law expires after 10 years unless voters extend it.  
>   
> **Yes to a large-estate climate contribution for a livable future.**

The campaign slogan could be:

> **“Small inheritances: untouched. Large fortunes: pay for the future their heirs will inherit.”**

Or, more Swiss:

> **“Keine Erbschaftssteuer für normale Familien. Ein Klimabeitrag für grosse Vermögen.”**

## Was it a mistake for voters to say no?

My honest answer: **No, I would not call it a mistake for voters to say no to the specific initiative.** Swiss voters have every democratic right to reject a tax proposal, especially one that may have sounded like:

- a new federal tax;
- a threat to family businesses and farms;
- a possible double tax alongside cantonal inheritance tax;
- a vague promise of climate spending without visible local projects;
- another top-down climate measure without a broad coalition.

If the choice was “accept this version or keep the status quo,” a large number of voters would rationally choose status quo. That does not mean they were anti-climate. It means the proposal did not remove their legitimate fears.

But I would say this:

**It would be a mistake if the “no” is now interpreted as a rejection of the principle.**

For example, it would be a mistake if the conclusion becomes:

- “The wealthy should not pay for climate.”
- “Inheritance is never a fair source of public revenue.”
- “Climate action must not cost anything visible to the rich.”
- “If one climate finance measure fails, all climate finance is dead.”

That would be the real mistake.

The voters likely did not say:

> “No to climate fairness.”

They probably said:

> “Not this design, not this framing, not this risk, not this trust level.”

That is a much more useful result.

## The positive spin, even if it stings

The initiative may have lost the vote, but it likely won the argument in the long run. It forced Swiss politics to confront something that had been undercooked for years:

> Climate action needs fair financing, and large inherited wealth should not be automatically excluded from that debate.

Before the initiative, many people could have avoided the question. Now they cannot. The next version does not have to start from zero. It can start from the lessons:

- higher threshold;
- no double taxation;
- family business protection;
- transparent climate fund;
- 10-year sunset;
- visible projects;
- broader coalition beyond the left.

So, if I had to sum it up:

**The voters were not mistaken to reject a flawed or fragile tax proposal. But the movement would be mistaken to treat the defeat as final. The inheritance idea did not die in November 2025; it became the strongest version of itself.**
